question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Odile Pelletier, a transportation engineer, has argued that narrowing the travel lanes on a city's arterial streets lowers crash rates by reducing the speeds at which drivers travel.
• The Corbeck Transport Institute studied eight arterial streets in the city of Kelsingham whose travel lanes were narrowed from 12 feet to 10.5 feet.
• Radar counts taken at the same three points on each street showed median speeds of 41 miles per hour before the lanes were narrowed and 35 miles per hour after.
• Crash records for the eight streets showed 3.1 crashes per million vehicle-miles traveled in the year before the lanes were narrowed and 3.1 in the year after.
• The radar counts were taken on weekday mornings between 9 a.m. and 11 a.m.
• The crash records came from the Kelsingham police department's incident database.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the institute's findings indicate about Pelletier's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The institute's findings support Pelletier's claim about driver speeds but not her claim about crash rates: median speeds fell from 41 to 35 miles per hour, but the crash rate stayed at 3.1 per million vehicle-miles traveled.
answer_b: The institute's findings bear out Pelletier's claim: on the eight streets whose lanes were narrowed, median speeds fell from 41 miles per hour before the change to 35 miles per hour after it.
answer_c: The institute's findings undermine Pelletier's claim: on the eight streets whose lanes were narrowed, the crash rate was 3.1 crashes per million vehicle-miles traveled both before and after the change.
answer_d: The institute's findings support Pelletier's claim about crash rates but not her claim about driver speeds: the crash rate stayed at 3.1 per million vehicle-miles traveled, but median speeds fell from 41 to 35 miles per hour.
explanation: Choice A is the best answer because it recognizes that Pelletier's claim has two parts and that the findings bear on them differently. Pelletier argues that narrowing lanes reduces drivers' speeds and that this lowers crash rates. The radar counts show that the first part happened: median speeds fell from 41 miles per hour to 35 miles per hour after the lanes were narrowed. The crash records show that the second part did not: the rate was 3.1 crashes per million vehicle-miles traveled both before and after. So the findings support the claim about speeds but not the claim about crash rates Choice A is the only choice that matches each set of data to the right part of the claim.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It accurately reports that median speeds fell from 41 to 35 miles per hour, but it ignores the crash records. Pelletier claims that the lower speeds lower crash rates, and the crash rate did not change, so saying the findings bear out the claim overall mistakes support for one part of the claim for support of the whole.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It accurately reports that the crash rate stayed at 3.1 per million vehicle-miles traveled, but it ignores the radar counts, which show that speeds did fall from 41 to 35 miles per hour. Because the findings do bear out the part of Pelletier's claim about speeds, saying only that they undermine the claim overstates how much the findings count against it.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It reverses which data bear on which part of the claim. The unchanged crash rate of 3.1 per million vehicle-miles traveled does not support Pelletier's claim about crash rates, since she claims the rate would fall. The drop in median speeds from 41 to 35 miles per hour does not count against her claim about speeds, since she claims that speeds would fall.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2019, agricultural economist Wenna Dorrigan claimed that moving a dairy farm from continuous grazing to rotational grazing raises the amount of forage its pastures produce and lowers the farm's spending on purchased feed.
• Researchers at the Corrin Dairy Research Station followed 18 dairy farms in the Lower Harrow district that switched to rotational grazing between 2021 and 2023.
• Farm accountants recorded each farm's purchased-feed spending, averaged across its herd: $212 per cow per year in 2021 and $214 per cow per year in 2023.
• The farms ranged in size from 40 to 130 cows, and all of them kept the same breed of cattle throughout the study.
• Technicians clipped and weighed forage from sample plots in every pasture each spring; average forage production was 3.1 tonnes of dry matter per hectare in 2021 and 4.0 tonnes per hectare in 2023.
• Each farm was visited by the same two technicians in both years.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the research team's findings indicate about Dorrigan's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The findings undermine Dorrigan's claim: on the 18 farms, purchased-feed spending did not fall after the switch to rotational grazing; it was $212 per cow per year in 2021 and $214 in 2023.
answer_b: The findings support Dorrigan's claim about forage but not her claim about feed spending: on the 18 farms, forage production rose from 3.1 to 4.0 tonnes per hectare, while spending was $212 per cow per year in 2021 and $214 in 2023.
answer_c: The findings support Dorrigan's claim about feed spending but not her claim about forage: on the 18 farms, spending went from $212 to $214 per cow per year, while forage production rose from 3.1 to 4.0 tonnes per hectare.
answer_d: The findings bear out Dorrigan's claim: on the 18 farms, average forage production rose from 3.1 tonnes of dry matter per hectare in 2021 to 4.0 tonnes in 2023 after the switch to rotational grazing.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it treats the two things Dorrigan says rotational grazing does as separate claims and tests each against the matching data. Dorrigan claims that the switch raises forage production, and the notes show that average forage production on the 18 farms rose from 3.1 tonnes of dry matter per hectare in 2021 to 4.0 tonnes in 2023, which fits that part. She also claims that the switch lowers purchased-feed spending, but the notes show spending of $212 per cow per year in 2021 and $214 in 2023, so spending did not fall. The findings therefore support the claim about forage but not the claim about feed spending.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It cites accurate spending figures, which do fail to show the lower spending Dorrigan claims, but it uses them to say the findings undermine the claim as a whole. It ignores the forage data, which show the rise in forage production that is the other thing Dorrigan claims, so it overstates how far the findings go against her.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It reverses which part of the claim each data point bears on. The forage increase from 3.1 to 4.0 tonnes per hectare is evidence for Dorrigan's claim that forage production rises, not evidence against it, and spending that went from $212 to $214 per cow does not show the lower spending she claims.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It cites accurate forage figures, which do fit Dorrigan's claim that rotational grazing raises forage production, but it says the findings bear out the claim as a whole. It ignores the spending data, which show spending going from $212 to $214 per cow rather than falling, so the part of her claim about lowering feed spending is not borne out.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 1974, art historian Agnete Tamsvik proposed that the Hessick ewer, a bronze water vessel in the Pellisham Museum's collection, was cast in a Kharsun Valley workshop in the twelfth century.
• In 2022, a team led by conservator Tomas Aldric ran two sets of laboratory tests on the ewer.
• Lead-isotope ratios in the ewer's metal match those of ore from the Kharsun Valley mines and differ clearly from those of ore from the neighboring Dovrin basin.
• Thermoluminescence testing of the clay core left inside the ewer's body from its original casting gave a firing date between 1390 and 1430.
• The Pellisham Museum acquired the ewer in 1931.
• The ewer stands 31 centimeters tall and weighs 2.4 kilograms.

The student wants to accurately characterize what Aldric's team's findings indicate about Tamsvik's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings support Tamsvik's claim about when the ewer was cast but not her claim about where: the core's firing date of 1390 to 1430 bears out the period, whereas the isotope ratios matching Kharsun Valley ore rather than Dovrin basin ore do not.
answer_b: The team's findings bear out Tamsvik's claim as a whole: the lead-isotope ratios in the ewer's metal match ore from the Kharsun Valley mines rather than ore from the neighboring Dovrin basin, which is consistent with a Kharsun Valley workshop.
answer_c: The team's findings support Tamsvik's claim about where the ewer was cast but not her claim about when: the isotope ratios match Kharsun Valley ore rather than Dovrin basin ore, whereas the core's firing date of 1390 to 1430 does not bear out the period.
answer_d: The team's findings undermine Tamsvik's claim as a whole: thermoluminescence testing of the clay core left from the ewer's original casting gave a firing date between 1390 and 1430, which conflicts with Tamsvik's proposed date for the ewer.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer because Tamsvik's 1974 claim contains two separate assertions: that the ewer was cast in a Kharsun Valley workshop (where) and that it was cast in the twelfth century (when). The notes bear on these differently. The lead-isotope ratios match Kharsun Valley ore and differ clearly from Dovrin basin ore, which is consistent with the Kharsun Valley origin. The thermoluminescence date of 1390 to 1430 falls in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, not the twelfth, so it does not bear out the claimed period. Choice C is the only choice that supports the place and not the period, and it cites both findings accurately.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it swaps which finding bears on which part of the claim. A firing date of 1390 to 1430 falls in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, so it cannot bear out a twelfth-century date, and the isotope match to Kharsun Valley ore supports, rather than weakens, the claim about where the ewer was made.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it treats the isotope match as confirming the whole claim. The ratios speak only to where the metal came from; they say nothing about when the ewer was cast, and the core's firing date of 1390 to 1430 does not fit the twelfth century. Citing only the supporting data leaves out the part of the claim the findings fail to bear out.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it treats the date as undermining the whole claim. The firing date of 1390 to 1430 conflicts only with the claim about when the ewer was cast; the isotope ratios still match Kharsun Valley ore, so the claim about where the ewer was made is borne out, and the findings do not undermine the claim as a whole.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In a 2021 paper, education researcher Dalia Fennimore claimed that weekly low-stakes retrieval quizzes in secondary-school courses raise students' unit-test scores and that the advantage is still present a year later.
• In 2025, a team led by Henrik Weyland tested the quizzes in 60 eleventh-grade chemistry sections across 12 schools in the Wrexley District, assigning sections to quizzes or no quizzes by lottery.
• Every section used the same textbook, and the unit tests were scored by graders who did not know which sections had taken quizzes.
• On the end-of-unit test, sections that took the weekly quizzes averaged 78 out of 100, and sections that did not averaged 67.
• A year later, 304 of the original students took a cumulative chemistry exam; the former quiz sections and the former non-quiz sections both averaged 64 out of 100.

The student wants to accurately characterize what Weyland's team's findings indicate about Fennimore's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: Weyland's team's findings refute Fennimore's claim: when the 304 students who returned a year later took a cumulative chemistry exam, the former quiz sections and the former non-quiz sections both averaged 64 out of 100.
answer_b: Weyland's team's findings bear out Fennimore's claim: in the 60 sections they tested, those that took the weekly quizzes averaged 78 out of 100 on the end-of-unit test, while those that did not averaged 67.
answer_c: Weyland's team's findings support Fennimore's claim that the advantage lasts but not her claim that quizzes raise scores: quiz sections averaged 78 out of 100 on the end-of-unit test to the others' 67, yet both groups averaged 64 a year later.
answer_d: Weyland's team's findings support Fennimore's claim that quizzes raise scores but not her claim that the advantage lasts: quiz sections averaged 78 out of 100 on the end-of-unit test to the others' 67, yet both groups averaged 64 a year later.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer because Fennimore's claim combines two separate assertions: that weekly retrieval quizzes raise unit-test scores, and that the advantage is still present a year later. The notes bear on these differently. On the end-of-unit test, quiz sections averaged 78 out of 100 against 67 for sections without quizzes, which supports the claim that the quizzes raise scores. A year later, however, the former quiz sections and the former non-quiz sections both averaged 64 on the cumulative exam, so there was no remaining advantage. The findings therefore support the first assertion but not the second, and Choice D cites both pieces of data to say so.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. The data it cites is accurate, but it treats the year-later result as if it disproved the whole claim. The equal averages of 64 show only that the advantage did not last. They do nothing to contradict the claim that the quizzes raise unit-test scores, which the 78 versus 67 result on the end-of-unit test supports. This is a conclusion drawn from only the data that fails one part of the claim.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. The data it cites is accurate, but it treats the end-of-unit result as if it confirmed the whole claim. The 78 versus 67 gap supports only the assertion that the quizzes raise unit-test scores. Fennimore also claimed the advantage is still present a year later, and the notes show the groups both averaging 64 on the cumulative exam. This is a conclusion drawn from only the data that fits one part of the claim.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it matches the data to the wrong parts of the claim. The 78 versus 67 gap on the end-of-unit test is evidence of an immediate gain, so it supports the claim that quizzes raise scores rather than contradicting it. The equal averages of 64 a year later show that no advantage remained, so they contradict the claim that the advantage lasts rather than supporting it. The choice reverses which assertion each result bears on.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 1998, geologist Teodor Roddam proposed that the granite boulders scattered across Kesmere Terrace were torn from the Tolsk Range, which rises 60 km to the northeast, and carried to the terrace by glacial ice.
• In 2022, a team led by geologist Mirela Talvane examined 40 granite boulders, each more than 1 meter across, at five sites on Kesmere Terrace.
• Zircon crystals in the 40 boulders have uranium-lead ages of 311 to 314 million years, matching the ages of zircon in the granite of the Tolsk Range.
• Apart from the Tolsk Range, granite exposed within 200 km of the terrace has zircon ages above 1 billion years.
• Thirty-eight of the 40 boulders have smoothly rounded corners and edges, and none of the 40 has parallel scratch marks on its surface.
• The boulders' surfaces show no weathering rinds or crumbling of mineral grains, which granite rounded in place by weathering typically shows.
• Rock fragments transported by glacial ice typically keep angular or subangular edges, and many carry parallel scratches from being dragged across bedrock.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Roddam's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings undermine Roddam's claim, since 38 of the 40 boulders have smoothly rounded corners and edges and none of the 40 has parallel scratch marks on its surface.
answer_b: The team's findings support Roddam's claim about the boulders' source but not his claim about how they were moved, since the zircon ages match those of the Tolsk Range granite while 38 of the 40 boulders are rounded and none is scratched.
answer_c: The team's findings support Roddam's claim about how the boulders were moved but not his claim about their source, since the boulders are rounded and unscratched while their zircon ages differ from those of the other granite exposed within 200 km of the terrace.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out Roddam's claim, since the zircon crystals in the 40 boulders have ages of 311 to 314 million years that match those of the Tolsk Range granite.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it recognizes that Roddam's claim combines two separate assertions, that the boulders came from the Tolsk Range and that glacial ice carried them, and that the findings bear on the two assertions differently. On the question of source, the zircon crystals in the boulders have ages of 311 to 314 million years, which matches the Tolsk Range granite, while the other granite exposed within 200 km has zircon ages above 1 billion years. That supports the Tolsk Range as the origin. On the question of transport, the notes say ice-carried fragments typically keep angular or subangular edges and often bear parallel scratches. Yet 38 of the 40 boulders have smoothly rounded corners and edges, and none has scratch marks. That does not fit transport by glacial ice. So the findings support the claim about the source but not the claim about how the boulders were moved.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. The rounded edges and absence of scratch marks do count against glacial transport, but they bear only on how the boulders were moved. Choice A treats that evidence as undermining the whole claim and ignores the zircon ages, which match the Tolsk Range granite and so support the claim about the boulders' source.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it reverses both verdicts. The rounded, unscratched surfaces do not fit the angular, scratched fragments that glacial ice typically leaves, so they count against Roddam's claim about how the boulders were moved rather than supporting it. And zircon ages that differ from those of other granite within 200 km do not count against the source: the boulders' ages match the Tolsk Range granite, so that difference actually strengthens Roddam's claim about where the boulders came from.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. The matching zircon ages do support the claim that the boulders came from the Tolsk Range, but they say nothing about what carried the boulders. Choice D treats that evidence as bearing out the whole claim and ignores the rounded, unscratched boulders, which do not fit the ice transport that Roddam also proposed.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Lye dipping is a baking step in which shaped dough is briefly immersed in an alkaline solution just before it goes into the oven.
• Food historian Piet Vossen proposed that the bakers of Calderwick dipped their rolls in a lye solution and that the dip is what gave the rolls their notably firm, chewy interior.
• A team led by chemist Sunniva Holtby examined twelve crust fragments from preserved Calderwick rolls; eleven contained sodium carbonate residue, which flour and water alone do not leave behind.
• The team also baked two batches of rolls from the same dough in the same oven: one batch was dipped in a lye solution beforehand, and the other was not dipped.
• A texture analyzer measured the force needed to compress each roll's interior by one centimeter: the dipped rolls averaged 41 newtons.
• Measured the same way, the undipped rolls also averaged 41 newtons.
• Both batches were baked for 22 minutes.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Vossen's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The findings support Vossen's claim about the bakers' practice but not his claim about the rolls' texture: eleven of the twelve preserved fragments contained sodium carbonate residue, while the dipped and undipped test rolls both averaged 41 newtons.
answer_b: The findings support Vossen's claim about the rolls' texture but not his claim about the bakers' practice: the dipped and undipped test rolls both averaged 41 newtons, while only eleven of the twelve preserved fragments contained sodium carbonate residue.
answer_c: The findings bear out Vossen's claim: eleven of the twelve crust fragments from preserved Calderwick rolls contained sodium carbonate residue, which flour and water alone do not leave behind.
answer_d: The findings undermine Vossen's claim: the dipped and undipped test rolls, made from the same dough and baked in the same oven, both needed an average of 41 newtons to compress their interiors by one centimeter.
explanation: Choice A is the best answer because Vossen's claim combines two assertions: that Calderwick bakers dipped their rolls in lye, and that the dip is what gave the rolls their firm, chewy interior. The notes bear on these differently. Eleven of the twelve preserved crust fragments contained sodium carbonate residue, which flour and water alone do not leave behind, so this supports the assertion that the bakers used the dip. But the team's two test batches, made from the same dough in the same oven, both needed an average of 41 newtons to compress their interiors. Because the undipped rolls were just as firm as the dipped ones, the findings do not show that the dip is what produced the firm, chewy interior. Choice A is the only choice that supports the first assertion with the residue and withholds support from the second because of the equal measurements.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it reverses which findings bear on which assertion. The equal measurements of 41 newtons show that dipping made no difference to the interior, so they count against, rather than support, the claim about texture. And residue in eleven of twelve fragments is evidence that the bakers did dip their rolls; the one fragment without residue does not outweigh the other eleven, so the residue supports, rather than undercuts, the claim about the bakers' practice.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. The residue in eleven of twelve fragments does support the assertion that the bakers dipped their rolls, but it says nothing about what produced the rolls' firm, chewy interior. Choice C ignores the two test batches, whose equal measurements of 41 newtons fail to support the claim that the dip produced that texture, and so it wrongly says the whole claim is borne out.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it is incomplete. The equal measurements of 41 newtons do fail to show that the dip produced the firm, chewy interior, but the residue in eleven of twelve fragments supports the other assertion, that Calderwick bakers dipped their rolls. By leaving out the residue evidence, Choice D does not accurately characterize what the findings indicate about Vossen's claim as a whole.
